nameStory: The redpoll gets its name from the distinctive bright red or pinkish patch on the top of its head, called a "poll" in old English. This crimson cap stands out like a tiny beret against the bird's streaky brown and white plumage, making it unmistakable even from a distance.
description: The common redpoll is a small, energetic finch about the size of a goldfinch that visits New England during winter months. These northern birds have streaky brown backs, whitish undersides, and that telltale red cap that gives them their name. Males often show a rosy pink wash on their chest and rump, while females tend to be more subdued in coloring. They're highly social birds that travel in bouncing, chattering flocks.

idTips.label: Red forehead patch
idTips.description: A bright red or pinkish cap sits right on top of the head above the bill - this red "poll" is present on both males and females and looks like it was dabbed on with paint

idTips.label: Black chin spot
idTips.description: A small but distinct black patch under the bill on the chin, creating a sharp contrast against the pale throat feathers

idTips.label: Streaky plumage
idTips.description: Brown and buff streaks run down the back and sides, giving the bird a rumpled, textured appearance that feels cozy and winter-appropriate

idTips.label: Pink chest wash (males)
idTips.description: Adult males show a soft pink or rosy blush across the breast and sometimes the rump, most vibrant during breeding season

idTips.label: Small pointed bill
idTips.description: A sharp, conical yellow bill perfect for cracking seeds - noticeably smaller and more delicate than a house finch's bill

idTips.label: Flocking behavior
idTips.description: Almost always seen in groups that move together in undulating flight patterns, chattering constantly with tinkling calls that sound like scattered coins

habitat: Redpolls prefer open areas with scattered trees and shrubs, including weedy fields, brushy roadsides, and forest edges throughout New England. They're particularly drawn to areas with birch, alder, and other seed-producing trees and shrubs. During winter visits, you'll often find them at backyard feeders or foraging in overgrown fields where they can access dried seed heads.

seasonality.spring: Most redpolls head north to breeding grounds by April, though some may linger into early May. Look for flocks becoming smaller and birds showing brighter breeding plumage.
seasonality.summer: Redpolls are generally absent from New England during summer months, spending this time breeding in the far northern forests of Canada and Alaska.
seasonality.fall: The first redpolls may arrive in late October or November, depending on food availability in the north. Early arrivals often show fresher, more contrasted plumage.
seasonality.winter: Peak season for redpoll watching! Large flocks roam throughout New England, visiting feeders and foraging for seeds. Numbers vary dramatically from year to year based on northern food crops.

funFact: Redpolls can survive temperatures as low as -65°F by having special pouches in their throat where they can store seeds to digest later while staying warm in shelter - essentially carrying their own packed lunch for extreme weather!
confusionNotes: House finches and purple finches can cause confusion, but neither has the redpoll's distinctive red forehead cap combined with a black chin spot. Remember: "Red on the poll (top), black on the chin" - if you see both features together, it's definitely a redpoll.
contextualKnowledge: Redpolls are famous for their "irruptive" behavior - some winters bring massive flocks south while other years they're completely absent from New England. These population swings depend on seed crops in their northern range, making redpoll sightings especially exciting and unpredictable.
compareHints: While redpolls are the only species in their genus regularly found in New England, they're most similar to siskins and goldfinches in the same finch family. Unlike goldfinches, redpolls keep their streaky pattern year-round and have that diagnostic red cap, while siskins lack the red forehead and have more yellow in their plumage.
